subject: Computer Networking
title: Insider Threats
description: A short lesson to help you apply Insider Threats.

hook.text: Not all threats come from outside. Sometimes the person with the badge and the password is the danger.

buildup.text: Insider threats include disgruntled employees, careless contractors, or anyone with legitimate access who misuses it.

discovery.text: They bypass perimeter defenses because they're already inside. Firewalls and intrusion detection can't see them.

twist.text: Snowden had authorized NSA access. He downloaded millions of classified files without triggering any alarms.

climax.text: Least-privilege access, activity monitoring, and separation of duties reduce insider risk but can't eliminate it.

punchline.text: The biggest threat might already have the keys.

quiz.question: Why are insider threats difficult to detect?
options: Insiders have legitimate access that bypasses perimeter defenses
Insiders only attack from outside the network

details.summary: Insider threats come from employees, contractors, or partners who misuse their authorized access to harm the organization. Threats range from malicious data theft to accidental exposure from negligent behavior.
details.whyItMatters: Insider threats bypass perimeter defenses entirely because the threat actor already has authorized access. Detection requires monitoring behavior patterns rather than blocking unauthorized access.
takeaways: Insiders already have legitimate access past security perimeters
Threats include malicious theft and accidental negligent exposure
User behavior analytics detect anomalous access patterns

faq.question: How do you detect insider threats?
faq.answer: User behavior analytics establish baseline activity patterns and flag anomalies like accessing unusual files, downloading large amounts of data, or logging in at odd hours. Data loss prevention tools monitor for sensitive data leaving the organization.

faq.question: What causes insider threats?
faq.answer: Malicious insiders may be motivated by financial gain, revenge, or ideology. Negligent insiders accidentally cause breaches through poor practices like sharing credentials or misconfiguring systems. Compromised insiders have their credentials stolen by external attackers through phishing or malware.
